source_text: Cur non istas operationes angelicas credimus per dispensationem prouidentiae dei bene utentis et bonis et malis secundum inscrutabilem altitudinem iudiciorum suorum? siue instruantur hinc mentes mortalium siue fallantur siue consolentur siue terreantur, sicut unicuique uel praebenda est misericordia uel inroganda uindicta ab illo, cui misericordiam et iudicium non inaniter cantat ecclesia. ut uolet accipiat quisque quod dicam. si rebus uiuentium interessent animae mortuorum et ipsae nos, quando eas uidemus, adloquerentur in somnis, ut de aliis taceam, me ipsum pia mater nulla nocte desereret, quae terra marique secuta est, ut mecum uiueret. absit enim, ut facta sit uita feliciore crudelis usque adeo ut, quando aliquid angit cor meum, nec tristem filium consoletur, quem dilexit unice, quem numquam uoluit maestum uidere. sed profecto quod sacer psalmus personat, uerum est: quoniam pater meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me, dominus autem adsumpsit me. si ergo dereliquerunt nos parentes nostri, quomodo nostris curis et rebus intersunt? si autem parentes non intersunt, qui sunt alii mortuorum, qui nouerint, quid agamus quidue patiamur? Esaias propheta dicit: tu es enim pater noster, quia Abraham nesciuit nos, et Israhel non cognouit nos. si tanti patriarchae, quid erga populum ex eis procreatum ageretur, ignorauerunt, quibus deo credentibus populus ipse de illorum stirpe promissus est, quomodo mortui uiuorum rebus atque actibus cognoscendis adiuuandisque miscentur? quomodo dicimus esse eis consultum, qui obierunt, antequam uenirent mala, quae illorum obitum consecuta sunt, si et post mortem sentiunt quaecumque in uitae humanae calamitate contingunt? an forte nos errando ista dicimus et hos putamus quietos, quos inquieta uiuorum uita sollicitat? quid est ergo, quod piissimo regi Iosiae pro magno beneficio promisit deus, quod esset ante moriturus, ne uideret mala, quae uentura illi loco et populo minabatur? quae dei uerba ista sunt. haec dicit dominus deus Israhel: uerba mea, quae audisti et ueritus es a facie mea, cum audisti, quae locutus sum de loco isto et qui commorantur in eo, ut deseratur et in maledicto sit, et conscidisti uestimenta tua, et fleuisti in conspectu meo, et ego audiui, dixit dominus sabaoth. non sic, ecce ego adponam te ad patres tuos, et adponeris cum pace; et non uidebunt oculi tui omnia mala, quae ego induco in locum hunc et qui commorantur in eo. territus iste dei comminationibus fleuerat et sua uestimenta consciderat; et fit omnium malorum futurorum de properatura morte securus, quod ita requieturus esset in pace, ut illa omnia non uideret. ibi ergo sunt spiritus defunctorum, ubi non uident quaecumque aguntur aut eueniunt in ista uita hominum. quomodo ergo uident tumulos suos aut corpora sua, utrum abiecta iaceant, an sepulta? quomodo intersunt miseriae uiuorum, cum uel sua ipsi mala patiantur, si talia merita contraxerunt, uel in pace requiescant, sicut huic Iosiae promissum est, ubi mala ulla nec patiendo nec conpatiendo sustineant, liberati ab omnibus malis, quae patiendo et conpatiendo, cum hic uiuerent, sustinebant?
thought_title: The dead do not know what the living do
orientation: Augustine is answering the question whether the dead can know or be involved in the affairs of the living, arguing from Scripture and from his own mother's silence that they cannot.

lemmas.gloss: be present in, take part in

choices.why: Literal rendering of the adjective-noun pair; 'operations' preserves the active sense of operatio as workings or activities.

choices.english: through the dispensation of God's providence
choices.why: Dispensatio is a key term for God's ordered management; 'dispensation' is the standard literal equivalent and matches the theological register.
rejected: through the arrangement of God's providence
through the stewardship of God's providence

choices.english: according to the unsearchable depth of his judgments
choices.why: Altitudo literally means height or depth; 'depth' is the natural English idiom for God's judgments, and 'unsearchable' preserves the negative adjective.
rejected: according to the unsearchable height of his judgments
according to the unfathomable depth of his judgments

choices.why: Directly echoes the psalm verse; both nouns are kept literal.
Pius here means devoted, dutiful, loving; 'pious' is the literal cognate and fits Augustine's affectionate reference to Monica.
The phrase is a fixed liturgical and biblical idiom; literal rendering preserves the echo of the promise to Josiah.

pass_b_english: Why should we not believe that these angelic operations happen through the dispensation of God's providence, who uses both good and evil well, according to the unsearchable depth of his judgments? Whether the minds of mortals are instructed by them, or deceived, or comforted, or terrified—as mercy is to be offered to each one, or punishment inflicted, by him to whom the church not in vain sings of mercy and judgment. Let each person take what I say as he will. If the souls of the dead were present in the affairs of the living, and they themselves spoke to us when we see them in dreams—to say nothing of others—my pious mother would not desert me on any night, she who followed me by land and sea so that she might live with me. Far be it that she became cruel in a happier life, to such a degree that when something troubles my heart she would not console her grieving son, whom she loved uniquely, whom she never wanted to see sorrowful. But surely what the holy psalm sounds forth is true: "For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up" (Psalm 27:10). If therefore our parents have forsaken us, how are they present in our cares and affairs? But if parents are not present, who are the other dead who know what we are doing or suffering? The prophet Isaiah says: "For you are our Father, because Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not recognize us" (Isaiah 63:16). If such great patriarchs did not know what was happening to the people begotten from them—the very people promised from their stock to those believing in God—how do the dead mix themselves into the affairs and actions of the living, to know and help them? How do we say that those who died before the evils came which followed their death were spared, if even after death they feel whatever happens in the calamity of human life? Or perhaps we say these things in error, and think those are at rest whom the restless life of the living disturbs? What then is this, that God promised the most pious king Josiah as a great benefit that he would die before seeing the evils that threatened to come upon that place and people? These are the words of God: "Thus says the Lord God of Israel: My words which you have heard, and you feared before my face when you heard what I spoke about this place and those who dwell in it, that it should be deserted and be under a curse, and you tore your garments and wept in my sight, and I have heard—says the Lord of hosts. Not so: behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered in peace; and your eyes shall not see all the evils which I am bringing upon this place and those who dwell in it" (2 Kings 22:19-20). Terrified by God's threats, he had wept and torn his garments; and he is made secure from all future evils by his hastening death, because he would rest in peace in such a way that he would not see all those things. There, then, are the spirits of the dead, where they do not see whatever is done or happens in this life of human beings. How then do they see their tombs or their bodies, whether they lie cast aside or buried? How are they present in the misery of the living, when either they themselves suffer their own evils, if they have contracted such deserts, or they rest in peace, as was promised to this Josiah, where they endure no evils either by suffering or by compassion—freed from all the evils which, while they lived here, they endured by suffering and by compassion?

last_rejected.source_quote: quoniam pater meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me, dominus autem adsumpsit me
last_rejected.why: Psalm 27:10 does not match; this verse is Psalm 27:10 in LXX/Hebrew numbering is wrong; correct is Psalm 27(26):10 or Hebrew 27:10
last_rejected.ruling: Psalm 27:10 is correct Hebrew numbering; LXX/Vulgate 26:10. Parenthetical note style acceptable; no meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: as mercy is to be offered to each one, or punishment inflicted
last_rejected.source_quote: sicut unicuique uel praebenda est misericordia uel inroganda uindicta ab illo
last_rejected.why: The Latin says mercy or vengeance is to be given/inflicted BY HIM (ab illo, i.e., by God), not that the church offers mercy or inflicts punishment. The English makes it passive without agent, changing agency.
last_rejected.fix: as mercy is to be granted to each one, or vengeance inflicted by him
last_rejected.ruling: 'Ab illo' is rendered passively; agency by God is implicit. Not a major error—reader is not misled.

last_rejected.quote: to whom the church not in vain sings of mercy and judgment
last_rejected.source_quote: cui misericordiam et iudicium non inaniter cantat ecclesia
last_rejected.why: The Latin says the church sings TO HIM (cui, dative), not 'of' mercy and judgment. The English 'sings of' changes the sense; the church sings to God, singing that he is mercy and judgment.
last_rejected.fix: to whom the church not in vain sings mercy and judgment
last_rejected.ruling: 'Sings of mercy and judgment to him' is within normal range; 'sings of' does not break meaning or mislead.

last_rejected.quote: How do we say that those who died before the evils came which followed their death were spared
last_rejected.source_quote: quomodo dicimus esse eis consultum, qui obierunt, antequam uenirent mala, quae illorum obitum consecuta sunt
last_rejected.why: 'Esse eis consultum' means 'that it was provided for them' or 'that they were well advised/cared for'—i.e., that it was a benefit to them. 'Were spared' changes the sense; they weren't 'spared' in the sense of escaping punishment, but it was 'provided for' them as a benefit that they died before the evils came.
last_rejected.fix: How do we say that it was well for those who died
last_rejected.ruling: 'Esse eis consultum' = 'was well for them'; 'spared' captures dying before evils came. Within acceptable range.

last_rejected.quote: and you feared before my face
last_rejected.source_quote: et ueritus es a facie mea
last_rejected.why: 'A facie mea' means 'before my face' in the sense of 'in my presence' or 'at my appearance'—the English 'before my face' is literal but correct. No error.
last_rejected.ruling: Checker themselves says 'No error.' 'Before my face' is correct rendering of 'a facie mea'.
